::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## A gentle welcome before we begin

In [Module 03](../03-molecular-data-types/index.qmd) you met your first four commands —
`pwd`, `cd`, `mkdir`, `ls` — while setting up a project folder. This module builds on
that foundation and gives you the rest of the everyday toolkit: how a command is
actually *structured*, how to ask the computer for help, and the dozen or so commands
you'll reach for again and again.

Here's the reassuring truth: the command line looks intimidating, but it's really just
a **conversation**. You type an instruction, the computer does it and replies. You do
*not* need to memorise hundreds of commands — a small core does 90% of the work, and for
everything else, the computer has a built-in manual you'll learn to summon in a second.

Nobody is fluent overnight. But spend a little time here, keep the terminal open as you
work, and it stops feeling foreign surprisingly fast.
:::

## What you'll learn

By the end of this module you'll be able to:

1. Read the **anatomy of a command** — the command, its options (flags), and its
   arguments.
2. Use **`man`** (and friends) to look up *any* command's details yourself.
3. Confidently use the **essential commands** for moving around, managing files, and
   peeking inside them.
4. Save time with **Tab completion** and **command history**.
5. Recognise **pipes and redirection** — a taste of how commands combine into pipelines.

### Before you start

- You have a working terminal from [Module 01](../01-setup-environment/index.qmd)
  (Ubuntu/WSL on Windows, or Terminal on macOS).
- You've met `pwd`, `cd`, `mkdir`, and `ls` in
  [Module 03](../03-molecular-data-types/index.qmd) — we'll build straight on those.

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify — small differences between systems
Linux (including WSL) and macOS share the same core commands, but a few options differ
between them (Linux tools are mostly "GNU"; macOS tools are mostly "BSD"). Where it
matters, we'll flag it. When in doubt, **`man` is always the source of truth for *your*
machine** — which is exactly why we teach it early.
:::

---

## Part A — The anatomy of a command

Almost every command you'll ever type follows the same simple pattern. Once you can see
the pattern, commands stop looking like magic spells and start looking like sentences:

![A command broken into its parts: the prompt, the command itself, its options/flags, and its argument.](img/anatomy-of-a-command.svg){width=820 fig-alt="Diagram labelling the parts of the command 'ls -lh ~/data'."}

Reading it left to right:

- **The prompt** (something like `you@computer:~$`) is printed *by the shell* to say
  "I'm ready." You don't type it — you type after it.
- **The command** is *what* you want to do (`ls` = list files).
- **Options** (also called **flags**) tweak *how* it's done. They usually start with a
  dash: `-l`, `-h`.
- **Arguments** are *what* you want to act on — here, the folder `~/data`.

### A word on flags

Flags come in three flavours, and you'll see all three:

| Style | Looks like | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Short** | one dash, one letter | `ls -l` |
| **Long** | two dashes, a whole word | `ls --all` |
| **Combined** | several short flags together | `ls -lh` (same as `ls -l -h`) |

::: {.callout-tip}
Order is usually flexible — `ls -l -h ~/data`, `ls -lh ~/data`, and often
`ls ~/data -lh` all work. And a command with **no arguments** just acts on a sensible
default (plain `ls` lists your *current* folder).
:::

---

## Part B — Getting help: `man` and friends

You will never memorise every command and every flag — and you don't have to. Unix ships
with its own manual, and knowing how to open it is one of the most empowering skills a
beginner can have.

### `man` — the manual

**`man`** (short for **manual**) shows the official documentation for a command. Try:

```bash
man ls
```

The top of a manual page is always laid out the same way:

```text
LS(1)                       General Commands Manual                      LS(1)

NAME
     ls - list directory contents

SYNOPSIS
     ls [-@ABCF...abcd...1] [file ...]

DESCRIPTION
     For each operand that names a file of a type other than directory, ls
     displays its name ...
```

How to read it:

- **NAME** — the command and a one-line summary.
- **SYNOPSIS** — the *shape* of the command. Two conventions to know:
  square brackets `[ ]` mean **optional**, and `...` means **"one or more."** So
  `ls [file ...]` reads as "`ls`, optionally followed by one or more files."
- **DESCRIPTION / OPTIONS** — the detail, including what every flag does.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Moving around inside a `man` page
`man` opens a full-screen reader. A few keys are all you need:

- **Spacebar** — down a page · **`b`** — back a page
- **`/word`** then Enter — search for *word*; **`n`** jumps to the next match
- **`q`** — quit (back to the prompt)
:::

### Quicker help: `--help`

Many commands also print a short help summary if you add `--help`:

```bash
mkdir --help
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## ⚠️ Verify
`--help` works for most Linux (GNU) tools, but several **macOS** commands don't support
it (you'll get an error). On macOS, reach for `man` instead — it always works. This is a
common early "why doesn't this work?" moment, and now you know why.
:::

### "Where does this command live?" — `which`

`which` tells you which program actually runs when you type a name — handy for checking a
tool is installed and on your `PATH`:

```bash
which ls
which conda
```

---

## Part C — The essential commands

Here is the core toolkit, grouped by what you're trying to do. Skim it now; you'll
internalise these by *using* them, not by memorising the table.

### Looking around

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `pwd` | print working directory (where am I?) | `pwd` |
| `ls` | list files & folders | `ls -lh` |
| `cd` | change directory (move) | `cd ~/projects` |

Useful `ls` flags: **`-l`** (long, detailed list), **`-a`** (show hidden files, whose
names start with `.`), **`-h`** (human-readable sizes like `30K` instead of `30429`).

### Working with files and folders

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `mkdir` | make a folder | `mkdir data` |
| `touch` | create an empty file (or update its timestamp) | `touch notes.txt` |
| `cp` | copy a file | `cp a.txt b.txt` |
| `mv` | move **or rename** a file | `mv old.txt new.txt` |
| `rm` | remove (delete) a file | `rm junk.txt` |

- To copy or delete a **folder** and its contents, add **`-r`** (recursive):
  `cp -r data backup`, `rm -r oldfolder`.
- `mv` does double duty: move a file to a new folder, *or* rename it in place.

::: {.callout-warning}
## 🧰 `rm` is forever — handle with care
On the command line there is **no Recycle Bin / Trash**. `rm` deletes *immediately and
permanently*. Two habits keep you safe:

- Add **`-i`** to be asked for confirmation first: `rm -i file.txt`.
- Treat **`rm -rf`** (force, recursive) with real respect — it deletes a whole folder
  tree with no questions asked. Double-check the path *before* you press Enter.
:::

### Peeking inside files

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `cat` | print a whole file to the screen | `cat notes.txt` |
| `less` | view a big file one page at a time (press `q` to quit) | `less big.txt` |
| `head` | show the **first** lines (default 10) | `head -5 data.csv` |
| `tail` | show the **last** lines (default 10) | `tail -5 data.csv` |
| `wc` | count lines, words, characters | `wc -l data.csv` |

::: {.callout-tip}
For anything large — and biological data files are *huge* — use **`less`** or **`head`**,
never `cat`. `cat` dumps the entire file, which can flood your terminal with millions of
lines.
:::

### Finding things

| Command | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `grep` | search for text inside files | `grep "TP53" genes.txt` |
| `find` | search for files by name | `find . -name "*.fasta"` |

Handy `grep` flags: **`-i`** (ignore upper/lower case), **`-c`** (count matches instead
of showing them), **`-n`** (show line numbers). `grep` is one of the most useful
commands in all of bioinformatics — you'll meet it constantly.

### A few everyday conveniences

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `echo` | print text (e.g. `echo "hello"`) |
| `clear` | clear the screen (or press `Ctrl` + `L`) |
| `history` | show the commands you've run recently |

---

## Part D — Two genuine superpowers

These two habits save more time than any single command. Learn them today.

- **Tab completion.** Start typing a file or folder name and press **`Tab`** — the shell
  finishes it for you. Type `cd ~/proj` then Tab, and it completes to `~/projects/`. This
  prevents typos *and* saves enormous amounts of typing. (Press Tab twice to see all the
  options when there's more than one match.)
- **Command history.** Press the **Up arrow** to bring back your previous command (keep
  pressing to go further back). Perfect for re-running something, or fixing a small typo
  without retyping the whole line.

::: {.callout-tip}
Two more rescue keys: **`Ctrl` + `C`** cancels whatever is currently running (a lifesaver
when something hangs), and **`Ctrl` + `L`** clears the screen.
:::

---

## Part E — A first taste of pipes and redirection

You don't need these yet, but you'll see them everywhere in bioinformatics, so here's a
gentle preview of the idea: **small commands can be joined together.**

- A **pipe** (`|`) sends the output of one command straight into another:

  ```bash
  cat genes.txt | grep "TP53" | wc -l
  ```

  Read left to right: print the file → keep only lines with "TP53" → count them. Each
  command does one small job, and the pipe passes the result along.

- **Redirection** sends output into a *file* instead of the screen: **`>`** writes (and
  overwrites), **`>>`** adds to the end:

  ```bash
  grep "TP53" genes.txt > tp53_hits.txt
  ```

::: {.callout-note}
This is just a taste — we'll use pipes properly in later modules. For now, simply
recognise `|`, `>`, and `>>` when you see them: they're how a few simple commands become
a powerful pipeline.
:::

---

## Part F — Hands-on: put it together

Let's use the real reference file from Module 03. If you still have it, move into that
folder; if not, re-download it (Module 03, Part K). Then let's inspect it with the
commands you just met — this is exactly how you'd first "look at" any new data file.

```bash
cd ~/projects/covid-demo/references   # go where the file lives
ls -lh                                # what's here, and how big?
```

**Real output:**

```text
total 64
-rw-r--r--  1 you  staff   30K Aug 16 04:19 sars2.fasta
```

That long line is what `-l` gives you: permissions, owner, group, **size** (`30K`,
thanks to `-h`), the date, and the filename. Now peek inside:

```bash
head -2 sars2.fasta        # the first two lines
wc -l sars2.fasta          # how many lines?
grep -c "^>" sars2.fasta   # how many sequences? (FASTA headers start with ">")
```

**Real output:**

```text
>NC_045512.2 Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 isolate Wuhan-Hu-1, complete genome
ATTAAAGGTTTATACCTTCCCAGGTAACAAACCAACCAACTTTCGATCTCTTGTAGATCTGTTCTCTAAA
     430 sars2.fasta
1
```

In four short commands you found where the file is, how big it is, what its first lines
look like, that it has **430 lines**, and that it contains exactly **one sequence**.
That's the everyday rhythm of working with data on the command line — and you just did
it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## ✅ Check
If `grep -c "^>" sars2.fasta` printed `1`, and `wc -l` printed `430`, everything's
working. (Don't worry if the file's date or size differ slightly — yours will reflect
when *you* downloaded it.)
:::

---

## Recap

You now can:

- ✅ Read any command as **command + options (flags) + arguments**.
- ✅ Look up *anything* yourself with **`man`** (and `--help` / `which`).
- ✅ Use the core toolkit — `ls`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `cat`, `less`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`,
  `grep`, `find`, and friends — safely (including respecting `rm`).
- ✅ Move faster with **Tab completion** and **command history**.
- ✅ Recognise **pipes (`|`)** and **redirection (`>`, `>>`)** when you meet them.

That's genuinely most of what day-to-day command-line work involves. Everything else is
variations on this handful of ideas.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Keep going — a word of encouragement

If some of this still feels awkward, that's completely expected — the command line is a
skill, like riding a bike, and it clicks through *doing*, not reading. The single best
thing you can do now is **keep the terminal open** while you work and reach for it for
small tasks (listing a folder, peeking at a file) instead of the mouse. Within a couple
of weeks it'll feel like second nature, and you'll wonder how you managed without it.

And remember your safety net: whenever you forget what a command or flag does, **`man`**
is one word away. You're never stuck.
:::

## Exercises

1. Run `man wc`. Use it to find out what the **`-w`** flag does, then quit the manual
   with `q`.
2. In your `~/projects/covid-demo` folder, make a `notes.txt` with `touch`, write a line
   into it (`echo "my first note" > notes.txt`), then read it back with `cat`.
3. Copy `notes.txt` to `notes_backup.txt` with `cp`, then rename the copy to
   `archive.txt` with `mv`. Confirm with `ls`.
4. Use `head`, `tail`, and `wc -l` on your `references/sars2.fasta` file. How many lines
   does it have?
5. Practise **Tab completion**: type `cd ~/proj` and press Tab. Then press the **Up
   arrow** a few times to see your recent commands.
6. **Careful one:** delete `archive.txt` with `rm -i archive.txt` and notice how `-i`
   asks you to confirm first.

## Where to go next

You've now got a real command-line foundation — the structure of commands, the manual,
and the essential toolkit. Later modules lean on these constantly (aligning reads,
running pipelines, wrangling results), adding new commands a few at a time. New modules
appear on the [home page](../../index.qmd) as they're ready.

Best next step: **use these commands for real.** Poke around your own folders, look
inside files, and lean on `man` whenever you're unsure. The fluency comes from the doing.

::: {.callout-important}
## One more time on accuracy
Command options can differ slightly between Linux (GNU) and macOS (BSD), and tools are
occasionally updated. The authoritative reference for *your* machine is always **`man`**
(and each tool's official documentation) — it supersedes this tutorial whenever they
disagree.
:::
